questions.concept_tag: Synonyms - size word
questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to ENORMOUS.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: ENORMOUS means extremely large, and HUGE has the same sense. Reading signal: 'enormous' describes size, so look for the option that also describes great size. Trap (A): Tiny is the opposite of enormous; students pick it when they hurry and read the question as 'opposite in meaning'. Trap (B): Ordinary is chosen because the word norm hides inside e-NORM-ous, a false root; the word is not related to 'normal'. Trap (D): Famous mixes up 'big in size' with 'big in reputation'.

questions.concept_tag: Antonyms - time word
questions.question_text: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to ANCIENT.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: ANCIENT means belonging to a very distant past, so its opposite is MODERN, belonging to the present time. Reading signal: three options are about old things, so the odd one out is usually the answer to an 'opposite' question. Trap (B): Old is a synonym of ancient; students pick it by forgetting the question asks for the opposite. Trap (C): Historic relates to the past (and to important events), so it points the same way as ancient. Trap (D): Antique is another word for something old and valuable, so it is a near-synonym.

questions.concept_tag: Idioms - ease
questions.question_text: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: a piece of cake.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The idiom 'a piece of cake' means a task that is very easy to do, as in 'The test was a piece of cake'. Reading signal: when an idiom names a thing from daily life, the meaning is almost never about that thing; ask what the thing suggests (cake is easy to eat). Trap (A): A tasty dessert takes the words literally. Trap (B): A small share is drawn from the word 'piece'. Trap (C): A sweet surprise comes from linking cake with birthdays and gifts.

questions.concept_tag: Prepositions - clock time
questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: The meeting is scheduled ____ 10 a.m.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Use 'at' with an exact clock time (at 10 a.m., at noon, at midnight). Rule: at for clock times, on for days and dates, in for months, years and parts of the day. Trap (A): 'in' is used for 'in the morning', so students use it for any time word. Trap (C): 'on' is used for days (on Monday), and is wrongly extended to clock times. Trap (D): 'by' means 'not later than', which changes the meaning from a fixed time to a deadline.

questions.concept_tag: Error spotting - adjective used as adverb
questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) She sings / (B) very good / (C) and wins / (D) every contest.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The verb 'sings' needs an adverb to describe how she sings, so 'very good' must be 'very well'. Rule: an adjective describes a noun; an adverb describes a verb. Quick test: ask 'sings how?', and the answer is an adverb. Trap (A): 'She sings' is correct, since 'sings' agrees with 'she', but students distrust a verb that stands first. Trap (C): 'and wins' is correct and parallels 'sings'. Trap (D): 'every contest' is correct, since 'every' takes a singular noun.

questions.concept_tag: Synonyms - fragility
questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to FRAGILE.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: FRAGILE means easily broken or damaged, so BREAKABLE is the match. Reading signal: replace the word in 'a fragile glass' with each option and see which keeps the meaning. Trap (A): Rigid is close to the opposite, because a stiff object is the one that does not break easily. Trap (B): Bendable confuses flexibility with fragility; a bendable thing often survives a fall. Trap (C): Valuable comes from the 'Fragile' label on parcels, which is a label for delicate goods, not a meaning of the word.

questions.concept_tag: Idioms - secrecy
questions.question_text: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: to spill the beans.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'To spill the beans' means to let out a secret by accident or too early. Example: 'Ravi spilled the beans about the surprise party.' Reading signal: when the idiom involves spilling or letting go of something, the 'thing' is usually information. Trap (B): To cook a meal is drawn from the word 'beans'. Trap (C): To waste food comes from reading 'spill' literally. Trap (D): To make a mess keeps only the 'spill' part of the picture.

questions.concept_tag: Articles - a or an
questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: She is ____ honest girl, and everyone trusts her.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Honest' begins with a vowel sound because the h is silent (it sounds like 'onest'), so the article is 'an'. Rule: choose a or an by the first sound, not the first letter. Trap (A): 'a' is chosen because honest is spelt with the consonant letter h. Trap (B): 'the' is used for something already known or unique, and no particular girl was mentioned before. Trap (D): no article is wrong because a singular countable noun needs an article.

questions.concept_tag: Error spotting - uncountable noun
questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) The furniture in / (B) our new house / (C) are very / (D) comfortable.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Furniture' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb, so 'are' must be 'is'. The subject is 'furniture', not 'house', which only sits in a phrase that describes where the furniture is. Rule: furniture, luggage, advice, information and news always take a singular verb. Trap (A): 'The furniture in' is correct, and students distrust it because they expect the error where the subject is. Trap (B): 'our new house' is the noun that sits near the verb, but it is not the subject. Trap (D): 'comfortable' is a correct adjective after the verb.

questions.concept_tag: Sentence improvement - present perfect continuous with for
questions.question_text: Choose the best improvement for the underlined part. If no improvement is needed, choose 'No improvement'. She **have been** working here for ten years.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The subject 'she' is singular, so the helping verb must be 'has': 'She has been working here for ten years.' Rule: have goes with I, you, we, they; has goes with he, she, it. Trap (B): 'had been' changes the tense to the past perfect continuous, which would need a past reference point. Trap (C): 'is being working' is not a valid verb form. Trap (D): No improvement is chosen because 'have been working' sounds natural when it follows the plural 'they'.

questions.concept_tag: Prepositions - afraid of
questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: The little boy is afraid ____ the dark.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The adjective 'afraid' is followed by 'of': afraid of the dark, afraid of dogs. Rule: some adjectives have a fixed preposition (afraid of, fond of, jealous of, angry with, good at). Learn them as pairs. Trap (A): 'at' belongs to words like surprised at and good at. Trap (B): 'from' belongs to verbs of escaping, such as run away from. Trap (C): 'with' belongs to angry with and pleased with.

questions.concept_tag: Conditionals - third conditional
questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: I would have helped him if he ____ me earlier.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The main clause 'would have helped' describes an imagined past, so the if-clause needs the past perfect: 'if he had asked'. Pattern: if + past perfect, would have + past participle. Trap (A): 'asks' is the present tense, which belongs to the first conditional (if he asks, I will help). Trap (C): 'has asked' is the present perfect, which cannot sit with 'earlier' in an imagined past. Trap (D): 'would ask' is the most common slip, because students copy 'would' from the main clause into the if-clause.

questions.concept_tag: Idioms - rarity
questions.question_text: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: once in a blue moon.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Once in a blue moon' means something that happens very rarely. A blue moon is itself an uncommon event, so the phrase stands for rarity. Example: 'He visits us once in a blue moon.' Trap (B): Every month comes from the moon's monthly cycle. Trap (C): Only at night links the moon with darkness. Trap (D): When the sky is cloudy takes 'blue' as a colour of the sky.

questions.concept_tag: Sentence improvement - did not with a base verb
questions.question_text: Choose the best improvement for the underlined part. If no improvement is needed, choose 'No improvement'. He **did not went** to school yesterday.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: After 'did not' the main verb returns to its base form: 'did not go'. The helping verb 'did' already shows the past tense, so the main verb must not carry it again. Rule: did/does/do + not + base verb. Trap (A): 'does not went' mixes a present helper with a past main verb. Trap (B): 'has not went' wrongly uses 'went' as a participle; the participle of go is gone. Trap (C): 'was not go' joins the helper 'was', which needs -ing or a participle, with a base verb.

questions.concept_tag: Articles - superlative
questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: Rohan is ____ tallest boy in the class.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A superlative (tallest, best, fastest) singles out one item from a group, so it takes 'the': the tallest boy. Rule: always use 'the' before a superlative adjective. Trap (A): 'a' would suggest one of several boys equally tall, with no special position. Trap (C): No article is tempting because names and plural nouns often need none, but a singular noun cannot go without one here. Trap (D): 'an' is used only before a vowel sound, and 'tallest' begins with a consonant sound.

questions.concept_tag: Synonyms - commence
questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to COMMENCE.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: COMMENCE means to start, which is the same as BEGIN. Example: 'The ceremony will commence at noon.' Reading signal: commence and begin are a formal-informal pair, like purchase and buy. Trap (A): Conclude is the opposite, since it means to finish. Trap (B): Postpone means to put off to a later time, so the event does not start at all. Trap (D): Continue means to carry on after the start, not the start itself.

questions.concept_tag: Antonyms - position word
questions.question_text: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to EXTERIOR.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: EXTERIOR means the outside, so its opposite is INTERIOR, the inside. Reading signal: ex- means out and in- means inside, so the prefixes themselves show the contrast. Trap (A): Outer is a synonym of exterior. Trap (B): Surface is related to the outside of an object, and students pick it from that association. Trap (C): External is another synonym of exterior.

questions.concept_tag: Error spotting - tense with a past time word
questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) I have seen / (B) him yesterday / (C) at the / (D) railway station.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Yesterday' names a finished moment in the past, so the simple past is needed: 'I saw him yesterday'. The present perfect (have seen) cannot be used with words like yesterday, last week or in 2010. Rule: a definite past time word means the simple past tense. Trap (B): 'him yesterday' looks like the odd phrase, but it is correct and is the signal that tells you the tense of part A must change. Trap (C): 'at the' is a correct preposition with article. Trap (D): 'railway station' is a correct noun phrase.

questions.concept_tag: Prepositions - prefer to
questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: She prefers tea ____ coffee.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The verb 'prefer' is followed by 'to' when two things are compared: prefer tea to coffee. Rule: prefer ... to; never prefer ... than. Trap (A): 'than' is used after comparatives such as better and more, so students carry it over to prefer. Trap (C): 'from' belongs to words like different from. Trap (D): 'against' borrows the idea of weighing one thing against another, but the fixed pattern is prefer ... to.

questions.concept_tag: Sentence improvement - suggest that
questions.question_text: Choose the best improvement for the underlined part. If no improvement is needed, choose 'No improvement'. She **suggested me** to take a break.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Suggest' is not followed directly by an object and a to-infinitive; it takes a that-clause: 'She suggested that I take a break'. Rule: suggest + that + subject + base verb (or suggest + -ing). Compare tell, which does take 'tell me to'. Trap (A): No improvement is chosen because 'suggested me to' copies the pattern of 'told me to'. Trap (B): 'suggested me taking' keeps the wrong object after suggest. Trap (D): 'suggests me to take' repeats the same pattern error and also changes the tense.

questions.concept_tag: Synonyms - reducing severity
questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to MITIGATE.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: MITIGATE means to make something less severe or less painful, and ALLEVIATE means the same: 'Medicine can mitigate the pain.' Reading signal: test each option in the sentence 'The new rules will ___ the damage'; only 'alleviate' keeps the sense of reducing harm. Trap (A): Worsen is the opposite of mitigate; students who rush read the question as 'opposite in meaning'. Trap (B): Postpone is drawn from the sound of 'mitigate' being close to 'litigate', which brings up courts and delays. Trap (D): Justify comes from the legal phrase 'mitigating circumstances', which reduce blame; students think such circumstances justify the act, but they only soften the punishment.

questions.concept_tag: Antonyms - speech style
questions.question_text: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to VERBOSE.
questions.trap_type: Related word taken as the opposite
questions.pedagogical_explanation: VERBOSE means using more words than needed, so its opposite is CONCISE, using few words to say what matters. Reading signal: three options describe how much or how well someone speaks, so ask which one is about length; only concise is the true opposite. Trap (B): Wordy is a synonym of verbose. Trap (C): Talkative is close in meaning, since a talkative person tends to be verbose. Trap (D): Eloquent means fluent and persuasive; students treat it as the opposite because they confuse 'many words' with 'good words', but an eloquent speaker can be brief or long.

questions.concept_tag: Idioms - courage in hardship
questions.question_text: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: to bite the bullet.

options.B: To act in an aggressive manner
options.C: To get hurt in a fight
options.D: To face a painful situation bravely

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'To bite the bullet' means to accept an unpleasant but unavoidable situation and deal with it with courage. Example: 'He bit the bullet and told the manager about the mistake.' Reading signal: when an idiom pictures a hard, painful action, the meaning usually concerns endurance; the object (a bullet) is only a picture. Trap (A): To eat very quickly is drawn from the word 'bite'. Trap (B): To act in an aggressive manner is suggested by the violent word 'bullet'. Trap (C): To get hurt in a fight takes the bullet as a wound instead of as something to be endured.

questions.concept_tag: Subject-verb agreement - a number of vs the number of
questions.question_text: Fill in the blanks: A number of students ____ absent today, but the number of absentees ____ small.
questions.trap_type: Same rule applied to both phrases
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'A number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb: 'A number of students are absent'. 'The number of' points to one figure and takes a singular verb: 'the number of absentees is small'. Rule: a number of + plural verb; the number of + singular verb. Trap (A): is, is treats both phrases as singular because the word 'number' is singular. Trap (C): is, are reverses the two rules. Trap (D): are, are treats both as plural because the nouns 'students' and 'absentees' are plural.

questions.concept_tag: Error spotting - despite and in spite of
questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) Despite of the heavy rain, / (B) the match / (C) was held / (D) on schedule.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Despite' is never followed by 'of'; the correct forms are 'despite the heavy rain' or 'in spite of the heavy rain'. Rule: despite = in spite of, and the 'of' belongs only to the longer phrase. Trap (B): 'the match' is the singular subject and is correct. Trap (C): 'was held' agrees with 'match'; students look at the nearby word 'rain' and want a different verb, but the subject is the match. Trap (D): 'on schedule' is a fixed phrase meaning at the planned time; students are tempted to change the preposition to 'in'.

questions.concept_tag: Sentence improvement - senior to
questions.question_text: Choose the best improvement for the underlined part. If no improvement is needed, choose 'No improvement'. He is **senior than** me by two years.
questions.trap_type: Than used after a Latin comparative
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Words like senior, junior, superior, inferior and prefer come from Latin comparatives and take 'to', not 'than': 'He is senior to me'. Rule: senior, junior, superior, inferior + to. Trap (A): 'more senior than me' tries to build a comparative, but senior already carries the comparison in its meaning. Trap (B): 'senior than I' fixes the pronoun case but keeps the wrong word 'than'. Trap (D): No improvement is chosen because 'senior than' sounds like 'taller than', which is a regular adjective.

questions.concept_tag: Prepositions - sentenced to and in prison
questions.question_text: Fill in the blanks: The judge sentenced him ____ five years ____ prison.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A judge 'sentences someone to' a term, and the term is spent 'in prison': 'sentenced him to five years in prison'. Rule: sentence + to (the punishment); in prison for the place. Trap (A): for, in uses 'for' because the phrase 'punished for' is common, but the punishment itself is introduced by 'to'. Trap (C): to, to repeats 'to' in the second blank from 'sent to prison', but five years cannot go 'to' a prison. Trap (D): for, at makes both slips and also chooses 'at', which is used for points like stations, not for being inside a prison.

questions.concept_tag: Idioms - ignoring wrongdoing
questions.question_text: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: to turn a blind eye.

options.D: To pretend not to notice something wrong

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'To turn a blind eye' means to knowingly ignore something that is wrong or against the rules. Example: 'The guard turned a blind eye to the late arrivals.' Reading signal: the person does see the thing, and the eye is only 'blind' by choice. Trap (A): To lose one's sight takes 'blind' literally. Trap (B): To look away in shame brings in a feeling of shame that the idiom does not carry. Trap (C): To judge someone unfairly is drawn from the idea of 'justice is blind', which is a different phrase.

questions.concept_tag: Synonyms - no longer in use
questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to OBSOLETE.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: OBSOLETE describes something that is no longer used because something newer has replaced it, which is what OUTDATED means: 'Typewriters are obsolete.' Reading signal: ask 'was it replaced by something better?'; if yes, the word is obsolete. Trap (A): Primitive means belonging to an early stage of development; an obsolete machine was once modern, not primitive. Trap (B): Faulty means not working properly; an obsolete device may work perfectly well. Trap (D): Unusual means rare, while many obsolete things were once very common.

questions.concept_tag: Antonyms - clarity
questions.question_text: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to AMBIGUOUS.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: AMBIGUOUS means open to more than one meaning, so its opposite is EXPLICIT, stated so clearly that there is only one meaning. Reading signal: when three options all describe lack of clarity, the odd one out is the answer to an 'opposite' question. Trap (B): Doubtful suggests that the speaker is unsure, which is close to ambiguous. Trap (C): Vague is a near-synonym, meaning not clearly expressed. Trap (D): Uncertain is also close in meaning, so students who rush pick it by forgetting the question asks for the opposite.

questions.concept_tag: Conditionals - second conditional with I
questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: If I ____ you, I would accept the offer without delay.
questions.trap_type: Indicative used for an imaginary situation
questions.pedagogical_explanation: An imaginary situation in the present takes the subjunctive 'were' for every subject, including I: 'If I were you...'. Pattern: if + were (imaginary), would + base verb. Trap (A): 'am' is the real present and cannot describe something that is not true. Trap (B): 'was' is common in speech, but exam grammar needs 'were' in an imaginary if-clause. Trap (C): 'were to be' is used for a remote possibility in the future ('if it were to rain tomorrow'), not for imagining oneself as another person.

questions.concept_tag: Error spotting - one of the + plural noun
questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) One of the best / (B) player in the / (C) team was / (D) injured yesterday.
questions.trap_type: Verb blamed instead of the noun
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'One of the' must be followed by a plural noun: 'one of the best players'. The verb stays singular because the subject is 'one'. Rule: one of the + plural noun + singular verb. Trap (A): 'One of the best' is correct, and students distrust a sentence that starts with a superlative. Trap (C): 'team was' is correct because the verb agrees with 'one'; students see the word 'team' and want 'were'. Trap (D): 'injured yesterday' is correct, with a past participle and a past time word.

questions.concept_tag: Confused words - abstain, restrain, resist
questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: The doctor advised him to ____ from smoking.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Abstain from' means to keep oneself from doing something, as in abstain from smoking, alcohol or voting. Rule: abstain/refrain + from + -ing form. Check each option with 'from': only 'abstain' fits. Trap (A): Restrain means to hold back someone or something by force, and it is not used with 'from smoking'; it also sounds like 'refrain'. Trap (B): Retain means to keep, so the sentence would say the opposite. Trap (C): Resist takes a direct object ('resist the urge') and not 'from'.

questions.concept_tag: Sentence improvement - married to
questions.question_text: Choose the best improvement for the underlined part. If no improvement is needed, choose 'No improvement'. She is **married with** a doctor.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The adjective 'married' takes 'to': 'She is married to a doctor.' Rule: married to, engaged to, related to, devoted to. Trap (B): 'by' is used for who performs a wedding ('married by a priest'), not for the spouse. Trap (C): 'for' suggests a purpose, as in 'married for money', which changes the meaning. Trap (D): No improvement is chosen because 'with' sounds natural after words like 'together with' and 'lives with'.

questions.concept_tag: Error spotting - along with does not change the verb
questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) The teacher, along with / (B) her students, / (C) are going / (D) on a picnic.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The subject is 'the teacher', which is singular. 'Along with her students' is an added phrase and does not make the subject plural, so the verb must be 'is going'. Rule: with, along with, together with, as well as and in addition to do not change the number of the subject. Trap (A): 'The teacher, along with' is correct, since 'along with' is a preposition. Trap (B): 'her students,' is a correct part of the added phrase. Trap (D): 'on a picnic' is correct, and students sometimes want 'for a picnic' without any reason.

questions.concept_tag: Tenses - past perfect for the earlier action
questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: By the time the police arrived, the thieves ____.
questions.trap_type: Passive used with an intransitive verb
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Two past actions are given: arriving and escaping. The escape happened first, so it takes the past perfect: 'had escaped'. Rule: by the time + simple past in one clause, past perfect in the other. 'Escape' here has no object, so it cannot be made passive. Trap (A): 'had been escaped' is a passive form, which is not possible with the verb 'escape' used this way. Trap (C): 'have escaped' is the present perfect and does not fit a story in the past. Trap (D): 'were escaped' is a passive past, and it suggests someone else made them escape.

questions.concept_tag: Sentence improvement - stative verb with since
questions.question_text: Choose the best improvement for the underlined part. If no improvement is needed, choose 'No improvement'. I **am knowing** him since childhood.
questions.trap_type: Continuous form used with a stative verb
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Know' is a stative verb (it describes a state, not an action in progress) and is not used in the continuous form. A state that began in the past and still continues takes the present perfect with 'since': 'I have known him since childhood.' Rule: since + a point in time goes with the present perfect, and stative verbs (know, like, own, belong) avoid -ing forms. Trap (A): No improvement is chosen by those who think 'am ... -ing' shows something going on now. Trap (B): 'knew him since' uses the simple past, which cannot be paired with 'since' for a state that continues. Trap (D): 'had known him since' needs another past event as its reference point, and none is given.

questions.concept_tag: Confused words - principal and principle
questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: The ____ of the school addressed the assembly.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Principal' used as a noun means the head of a school or institution. 'Principle' means a rule or belief. The sentence needs a person, so the answer is 'principal'. Memory aid: the principal is your PAL. Trap (A): principle is the homophone that students pick by sound; it means a rule or a basic idea, not a person. Trap (B): principles is the plural of that homophone and has the same problem. Trap (C): principally is an adverb meaning mainly, and a noun is needed after 'the'.

questions.concept_tag: Idioms - exact remark
questions.question_text: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: to hit the nail on the head.

options.A: To say or do exactly the right thing

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'To hit the nail on the head' means to describe a problem or situation in exactly the right way. Example: 'You hit the nail on the head when you said the plan lacked money.' Reading signal: a hammer that strikes the nail squarely is a picture of accuracy. Trap (B): To work extremely hard is drawn from the effort of hammering. Trap (C): To repair something quickly comes from the carpentry picture. Trap (D): To hurt oneself by mistake is the literal outcome of hitting the wrong thing with a hammer.

questions.concept_tag: Synonyms - calming anger
questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to PLACATE.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: PLACATE means to calm someone who is angry, and PACIFY means the same: 'The manager tried to placate the angry customers.' Reading signal: both words contain the idea of peace (placid, pacify). Trap (A): Provoke is the opposite, since it means to make someone angrier. Trap (C): Punish suggests dealing with a wrongdoer, which does not calm anyone. Trap (D): Flatter is chosen because flattery is sometimes used to win someone over, but it means praising too much, not calming anger.

questions.concept_tag: Subjunctive - insist that
questions.question_text: Choose the best improvement for the underlined part. If no improvement is needed, choose 'No improvement'. The manager insisted that every employee **is present** at the meeting.
questions.trap_type: Tense copied from the main verb
questions.pedagogical_explanation: After verbs of insisting, demanding, suggesting and recommending, the that-clause takes the base form of the verb (the subjunctive): 'insisted that every employee be present'. Shortcut: insist/demand/suggest/recommend/propose + that + subject + base verb, whatever the tense of the main verb. Trap (A): 'was present' copies the past tense of 'insisted'; the subjunctive does not follow the tense of the main verb. Trap (B): 'will be present' uses the future because the meeting is yet to happen, but the clause states a demand, not a prediction. Trap (D): No improvement is chosen because 'is present' sounds natural in everyday speech.

questions.concept_tag: Error spotting - parallel verb forms after enjoy
questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) She enjoys to paint, / (B) singing and / (C) dancing / (D) in her free time.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Enjoy' is followed by a gerund (the -ing form), and the three activities in a list must have the same form: 'enjoys painting, singing and dancing'. So the error lies in part A, 'to paint'. Shortcut: for verbs like enjoy, avoid, finish, mind and practise, use -ing; then check that every item in the list matches. Trap (B): 'singing and' is correct and sets the pattern the other items should follow. Trap (C): 'dancing' is correct and parallel with singing. Trap (D): 'in her free time' is a correct adverbial phrase.

questions.concept_tag: Vocabulary in context - cure-all
questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: Many people treat herbal tea as a ____ for every illness, although no single remedy can cure all diseases.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A panacea is a remedy supposed to cure all troubles or diseases, which is exactly the claim made about herbal tea in the sentence. Reading signal: the phrase 'for every illness' and the clause 'no single remedy can cure all diseases' both point to a cure-all. Trap (A): Antidote counteracts a specific poison, not every illness. Trap (C): Placebo is a harmless dummy treatment with no real medicine in it; it is not claimed to cure everything. Trap (D): Vaccine prevents one particular disease and does not cure illnesses.

questions.concept_tag: Idioms - challenge
questions.question_text: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: to throw down the gauntlet.

options.B: To act in a careless manner

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'To throw down the gauntlet' means to challenge someone openly to a contest or a fight. In the past, a knight threw down his glove (gauntlet) to challenge an opponent. Example: 'The new company threw down the gauntlet to the market leader.' Shortcut: the gesture is an announced challenge, not a surrender or an ambush. Trap (A): To give up a fight reads 'throw down' as dropping or abandoning something. Trap (B): To act in a careless manner takes 'throw down' as tossing things about without care. Trap (C): To attack someone by surprise confuses a challenge, which is made openly, with a sneak attack.

questions.concept_tag: Synonyms - hard to understand
questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to ABSTRUSE.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: ABSTRUSE describes ideas that are hard to understand, as in 'an abstruse theory'. OBSCURE (unclear, difficult to grasp) is the closest meaning. Reading signal: put each option into 'an abstruse argument' and keep the one that still means 'hard to follow'. Trap (A): Abrupt begins like abstruse but means sudden. Trap (C): Absurd also begins with 'abs' and sounds similar, but it means ridiculous or illogical. Trap (D): Elementary is the opposite, meaning simple and basic.

questions.concept_tag: Antonyms - harmful or harmless
questions.question_text: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to BENIGN.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: BENIGN means harmless or kindly, and for a tumour it means not cancerous. Its opposite is MALIGNANT, meaning harmful or deadly. Reading signal: the Latin roots bene (good) and male (bad) show the contrast, benign versus malignant. Trap (B): Harmless is a synonym of benign. Trap (C): Gentle is a synonym for the everyday sense of benign, as in a benign smile. Trap (D): Mild is also a near-synonym, so students who forget that the question asks for the opposite pick it.

questions.concept_tag: Active-passive - question in present perfect
questions.question_text: Choose the correct passive voice of: 'Who has broken the window?'

options.A: By whom the window has been broken?
options.B: By whom had the window been broken?
options.C: By whom was the window broken?
options.D: By whom has the window been broken?

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Who has broken the window?' is in the present perfect, so the passive keeps 'has been' with the past participle: 'By whom has the window been broken?' Rule: a question beginning with 'who' becomes 'By whom' in the passive, and the question word order is kept, with the helping verb before the subject. Trap (A): 'By whom the window has been broken?' drops the question word order; the helping verb 'has' must come before 'the window'. Trap (B): 'By whom had the window been broken?' changes the tense to the past perfect. Trap (C): 'By whom was the window broken?' changes the tense to the simple past.

questions.concept_tag: Direct-indirect speech - future with pronoun shift
questions.question_text: Choose the correct indirect speech of: He said to me, 'I will help you tomorrow.'

options.A: He told me that he will help me the next day.
options.B: He told me that I would help him the next day.
options.C: He told me that he would help me the next day.
options.D: He told me that he would help you the next day.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The reporting verb is in the past, so 'will' shifts back to 'would'. The pronoun 'I' (the speaker) becomes 'he', and 'you' (the listener, which is me) becomes 'me'. The time word 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'. So: 'He told me that he would help me the next day.' Shortcut: check three things in order: tense, pronouns, time words. Trap (A): 'will help' keeps the original tense and is not backshifted to would. Trap (B): 'I would help him' swaps the two people; the speaker becomes 'he', not 'I'. Trap (D): 'he would help you' leaves 'you' unchanged, but the listener is the person reporting, so 'you' must become 'me'.

questions.concept_tag: Cloze - connector of contrast
questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: Rohit does not score high marks in tests; ____, he is the most hardworking boy in his class.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The two clauses pull in opposite directions: he does not score high, yet he works harder than anyone. A connector of contrast is needed, and 'nevertheless' (in spite of that) fits. Reading signal: decide the relationship between the two clauses (contrast, addition, cause, comparison) before looking at the options. Trap (A): Therefore shows a result, but hard work is not the result of low marks. Trap (C): Besides adds one more point in the same direction, but here the second point goes against the first. Trap (D): Likewise shows similarity, which is not the relationship between the clauses.

questions.concept_tag: Sentence rearrangement - clause order after a fixed opening
questions.question_text: The sentence begins with 'After a detailed inspection,'. Rearrange the parts to complete it: P: that the old bridge Q: the engineers declared R: was unsafe for heavy vehicles S: and recommended closing it
questions.pedagogical_explanation: After the opening phrase, the subject and verb come first: 'the engineers declared' (Q). 'Declared' needs a that-clause, so 'that the old bridge' (P) follows, then its verb phrase 'was unsafe for heavy vehicles' (R), and the sentence closes with the added action 'and recommended closing it' (S). Result: After a detailed inspection, the engineers declared that the old bridge was unsafe for heavy vehicles and recommended closing it. Shortcut: find the subject-verb pair first, then the part that completes the verb. Trap (B): PQRS starts with 'that the old bridge' and has nothing to introduce the clause. Trap (C): QRPS puts the verb phrase 'was unsafe...' before its subject 'the old bridge'. Trap (D): SQPR starts with 'and recommended closing it', which cannot open the sentence because it continues a verb that has not yet appeared.

questions.concept_tag: Phrasal verbs - tolerate
questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: I cannot ____ his rude behaviour any longer.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Put up with' means to tolerate or endure: 'I cannot put up with his rude behaviour.' Reading signal: 'cannot ___ his behaviour any longer' means 'cannot bear it'. Trap (A): Put off means to postpone, or to discourage someone. Trap (B): Put out means to extinguish a fire or to inconvenience someone. Trap (D): Put down means to insult, or to place something on a surface, and it does not mean to endure.

questions.concept_tag: Error spotting - double negative after unless
questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) You will fail / (B) in the examination / (C) unless you / (D) do not study hard.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Unless' already means 'if ... not', so a negative verb after it makes a double negative. The correct form is 'unless you study hard'. Rule: never use a negative verb in the clause that follows 'unless'. Trap (A): 'You will fail' is a correct main clause. Trap (B): 'in the examination' is a correct phrase. Trap (C): 'unless you' is correct; the fault lies in the verb that comes after it.

questions.concept_tag: Sentence improvement - would rather
questions.question_text: Choose the best improvement for the underlined part. If no improvement is needed, choose 'No improvement'. I **would rather to stay** at home than go out in this heat.
questions.trap_type: Infinitive with to after a modal phrase
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Would rather' is followed by the base form of the verb without 'to': 'I would rather stay at home than go out.' Rule: would rather, had better, can and must are followed by a bare verb. Trap (A): 'would rather staying' uses the -ing form, which does not follow 'would rather'. Trap (C): 'will rather stay' changes the fixed phrase 'would rather' into 'will rather', which does not exist. Trap (D): No improvement is chosen because 'prefer to stay' does take 'to', and students mix up the two patterns.

questions.concept_tag: Error spotting - verb after one of those who
questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) She is one of those students who is / (B) always ready to / (C) help classmates / (D) in difficulty.

options.A: She is one of those students who is

questions.pedagogical_explanation: In 'one of those students who ...', the pronoun 'who' refers back to 'students' (plural), not to 'one', so the verb must be plural: 'who are'. Rule: one of those + plural noun + who + plural verb. Contrast this with 'one of the students is...', where 'one' is the subject. Trap (B): 'always ready to' is correct. Trap (C): 'help classmates' is correct. Trap (D): 'in difficulty' is correct; it is a fixed phrase.

questions.concept_tag: Error spotting - the + adjective as a plural noun
questions.question_text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) The government should / (B) provide better schools / (C) because the poor / (D) has no other option.
questions.trap_type: Singular verb with a plural group
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'The poor' means poor people, a plural group, so it takes a plural verb: 'the poor have no other option'. Rule: the poor, the rich, the young and the old take plural verbs. Trap (A): 'The government should' is correct, since a modal verb has no number. Trap (B): 'provide better schools' is correct and agrees with 'should'. Trap (C): 'because the poor' is correct; students blame it because they expect a noun after 'the'.

questions.concept_tag: Prepositions - deprived of
questions.question_text: Fill in the blank: The citizens were deprived ____ their basic rights by the new order.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Deprive' takes the preposition 'of': 'deprived of their basic rights'. Rule: deprive, rob, relieve, cure and rid are followed by 'of'. Trap (A): 'from' goes with words like prevent from and protect from. Trap (B): 'with' goes with provide with and supply with, which are the opposite of deprive. Trap (D): 'off' is a spelling slip for 'of'; deprive is never followed by 'off'.

questions.concept_tag: Idioms - costly victory
questions.question_text: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom: a Pyrrhic victory.

options.A: A victory won at too great a cost
options.D: A victory won at the last moment

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A Pyrrhic victory is a win that costs so much that it is almost as bad as a defeat. The phrase comes from King Pyrrhus of Epirus, who won battles against Rome but lost most of his army. Example: 'The company won the case but spent all its money on legal fees, a Pyrrhic victory.' Shortcut: a proper-noun idiom hides a story, so recall the story. Trap (B): A victory won very easily is the opposite of a costly win. Trap (C): A victory won by cheating confuses 'costly' with 'unfair'. Trap (D): A victory won at the last moment links 'victory' with a close finish, which the idiom does not mean.

questions.concept_tag: Synonyms - stubbornness
questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to OBDURATE.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: OBDURATE means stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action, so STUBBORN is the match: 'an obdurate official who ignored every appeal'. Reading signal: the root 'dur' (hard, as in durable) hints at 'hard' in attitude. Trap (A): Obedient begins with the same 'ob' and sounds similar, but it means willing to follow orders, which is close to the opposite. Trap (B): Timid means shy and fearful and has no link with firmness of will. Trap (D): Merciful is the opposite in the 'hard-hearted' sense; students who half-remember that obdurate can mean unmoved by pity pick it.

questions.concept_tag: Antonyms - spending habits
questions.question_text: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to FRUGAL.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: FRUGAL means careful about spending money, so its opposite is LAVISH, spending or giving in a generous and extravagant way. Reading signal: three options are about being careful with money, so the odd one out is the answer to an 'opposite' question. Trap (A): Thrifty is a synonym of frugal. Trap (C): Miserly is an extreme form of frugality (unwilling to spend at all), so it points the same way. Trap (D): Careful is a near-synonym in a sentence about money and is chosen by students who forget that the question asks for the opposite.

questions.concept_tag: Sentence improvement - look forward to + gerund
questions.question_text: Choose the best improvement for the underlined part. If no improvement is needed, choose 'No improvement'. I am looking forward **to meet** you next week.
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In 'look forward to', the word 'to' is a preposition, not part of an infinitive, so it is followed by a noun or an -ing form: 'looking forward to meeting you'. Test: if you can replace the verb with a noun ('looking forward to the meeting'), the 'to' is a preposition. The same holds for object to, be used to and in addition to. Trap (A): No improvement is chosen because 'to meet' looks like a normal infinitive, as in 'I want to meet you'. Trap (B): 'for meeting' changes the fixed preposition. Trap (C): 'to have met' is a perfect infinitive, which suggests the meeting is already over.

questions.concept_tag: Percentages - total from the passed share
questions.question_text: In a test, 25% of the candidates failed and 600 candidates passed. How many candidates appeared in the test?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Passed = 100% - 25% = 75% of the total. So 75% of T = 600 and T = 600 ÷ 3/4 = 800. Shortcut: 75% = 3/4, so multiply the passed number by 4/3. Trap (B): 750 comes from adding 25% of the passed number to 600, using the wrong base. Trap (C): 625 comes from adding 25 candidates to 600, as though 25% meant 25. Trap (D): 2,400 comes from treating 600 as the failed 25% (600 ÷ 1/4).

questions.concept_tag: Profit & Loss - selling price from profit percent
questions.question_text: A shopkeeper buys a bag for ₹640 and sells it at a profit of 15%. What is the selling price of the bag?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Profit = 15% of 640 = 96, so SP = 640 + 96 = ₹736. Shortcut: 640 × 1.15 = 736 in one step. Trap (A): 655 comes from adding 15 rupees to the cost, treating 15% as ₹15. Trap (B): 544 comes from multiplying by 0.85, which is the selling price at a 15% loss. Trap (D): 96 is only the profit; the cost price was not added back.

questions.concept_tag: Simple Interest - rate from principal and amount
questions.question_text: A sum of ₹4,000 becomes ₹5,000 in 5 years at simple interest. What is the rate of interest per annum?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Interest = 5,000 - 4,000 = ₹1,000 over 5 years. Rate = (1,000 × 100) / (4,000 × 5) = 5% per annum. Shortcut: 1,000 is 25% of 4,000 over 5 years, so 25 ÷ 5 = 5. Trap (A): 25 is the total interest as a percentage of the principal; the time was never divided out. Trap (C): 4 comes from using the amount ₹5,000 as the principal in the denominator: 1,000 × 100 / (5,000 × 5). Trap (D): 20 uses the amount as the principal and also forgets to divide by time.

questions.concept_tag: Ratio - difference between two shares
questions.question_text: ₹7,200 is divided between P and Q in the ratio 5 : 7. How much more does Q get than P?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total parts = 5 + 7 = 12, so one part = 7,200 ÷ 12 = 600. Q gets 7 × 600 = 4,200 and P gets 5 × 600 = 3,000, so Q gets 4,200 - 3,000 = ₹1,200 more. Shortcut: (difference of ratio terms) × (one part) = 2 × 600. Trap (A): 3,000 is P's share, not the difference. Trap (B): 4,200 is Q's share, not the difference. Trap (C): 600 is one part; the ratio difference of 2 was ignored.

questions.concept_tag: Simplification - fraction of a fraction
questions.question_text: What is 3/4 of 2/5 of 320?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 2/5 of 320 = 128, and 3/4 of 128 = 96. Shortcut: 3/4 × 2/5 = 3/10, and 3/10 of 320 = 96. Trap (A): 128 is only 2/5 of 320; the 3/4 was skipped. Trap (C): 240 is only 3/4 of 320; the 2/5 was skipped. Trap (D): 368 comes from adding the fractions (3/4 + 2/5 = 23/20) and taking that fraction of 320 instead of multiplying them.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
answer = Fraction(3, 4) * Fraction(2, 5) * 320

questions.concept_tag: Time & Work - combined days
questions.question_text: A can finish a piece of work in 9 days and B can finish it in 18 days. In how many days will they finish it working together?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: In one day A does 1/9 and B does 1/18, together 1/9 + 1/18 = 3/18 = 1/6, so they take 6 days. Shortcut: take total work = 18 units; A = 2 units/day, B = 1 unit/day, together 3 units/day, and 18 ÷ 3 = 6. Trap (B): 13.5 is the simple average of 9 and 18; two workers together must beat the faster one. Trap (C): 27 is the sum of the two times. Trap (D): 4.5 is 9 ÷ 2, assuming both work at A's speed.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
answer = 1 / (Fraction(1, 9) + Fraction(1, 18))

questions.concept_tag: Pipes & Cisterns - leak time from delay
questions.question_text: A tap fills a tank in 6 hours. Because of a leak at the bottom, the tank takes 8 hours to fill. In how many hours can the leak alone empty the full tank?
questions.trap_type: Extra time taken as leak time
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Tap alone: 1/6 per hour. With the leak: 1/8 per hour. Leak rate = 1/6 - 1/8 = 1/24 per hour, so the leak alone empties the tank in 24 hours. Shortcut: take capacity = LCM(6, 8) = 24 units; tap = 4/h, net = 3/h, so the leak = 1/h and empties 24 units in 24 h. Trap (A): 2 is the extra time, 8 - 6. Trap (B): 14 adds 6 and 8. Trap (C): 48 multiplies 6 and 8.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
answer = 1 / (Fraction(1, 6) - Fraction(1, 8))

questions.concept_tag: Time, Speed & Distance - trains approaching each other
questions.question_text: Two stations are 360 km apart. Two trains start from them at the same time and move towards each other at 50 km/h and 70 km/h. After how many hours do they meet?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The trains approach each other, so the relative speed = 50 + 70 = 120 km/h. Time = 360 ÷ 120 = 3 hours. Shortcut: add speeds when moving towards each other, subtract when moving the same way. Trap (A): 7.2 is 360 ÷ 50, using only the slower train. Trap (B): 18 is 360 ÷ 20, subtracting speeds as if the trains moved in the same direction. Trap (D): 6 is 360 ÷ 60, using the average speed instead of the combined speed.

questions.concept_tag: Mensuration - fencing cost of a square from its area
questions.question_text: The area of a square field is 1,296 m². What is the cost of fencing it at ₹15 per metre?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Side = √1,296 = 36 m. Perimeter = 4 × 36 = 144 m. Cost = 144 × 15 = ₹2,160. Shortcut: recognise 36² = 1,296, then fencing needs the perimeter (4 × side), not the area. Trap (B): 540 uses one side only (36 × 15). Trap (C): 19,440 multiplies the area by ₹15. Trap (D): 1,080 uses half the perimeter (72 × 15).
questions.verify_code:
import math
side = math.isqrt(1296)
answer = 4 * side * 15

questions.concept_tag: Simplification - BODMAS order
questions.question_text: What is the value of 48 ÷ 6 × 2 + 5² - 3 × 4?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Powers first: 5² = 25. Then ÷ and × from left to right: 48 ÷ 6 = 8, 8 × 2 = 16, and 3 × 4 = 12. Finally + and -: 16 + 25 - 12 = 29. Shortcut: order is brackets, orders (powers), then division and multiplication left to right, then addition and subtraction. Trap (A): 17 comes from 48 ÷ (6 × 2) = 4, doing the multiplication before the division. Trap (B): 14 reads 5² as 10. Trap (C): 152 works strictly left to right, ignoring that × outranks + and -.

questions.concept_tag: Percentages - one quantity as a percent of another with units
questions.question_text: What percent of 1.2 kg is 300 g?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Convert to the same unit: 1.2 kg = 1,200 g. Percentage = (300 / 1,200) × 100 = 25%. Shortcut: 300 g is a quarter of 1,200 g. Trap (A): 250 divides 300 by 1.2 without converting units. Trap (B): 400 inverts the ratio (1,200 / 300 × 100). Trap (D): 2.5 over-converts, treating 1.2 kg as 12,000 g.

questions.concept_tag: Discount - marked price from selling price
questions.question_text: After a discount of 20% on its marked price, a television is sold for ₹16,000. What is its marked price?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The selling price is 80% of the marked price: 0.8 × MP = 16,000, so MP = ₹20,000. Shortcut: 80% = 4/5, so MP = 16,000 × 5/4. Trap (A): 19,200 adds 20% of the selling price (16,000 × 1.2); the discount was on the marked price, not the selling price. Trap (C): 12,800 applies the 20% discount a second time to the selling price. Trap (D): 3,200 is 20% of the selling price, which is not the marked price.

questions.concept_tag: Compound Interest - two years
questions.question_text: What is the compound interest on ₹6,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum, compounded annually?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Year 1 interest = 10% of 6,000 = 600, giving 6,600. Year 2 interest = 10% of 6,600 = 660. CI = 600 + 660 = ₹1,260. Shortcut: two successive 10% increases equal 21%, and 21% of 6,000 = 1,260. Trap (A): 1,200 is simple interest (600 a year for 2 years). Trap (B): 7,260 is the amount, not the interest. Trap (C): 1,320 doubles the second-year interest (660 × 2).
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
answer = 6000 * (Fraction(11, 10) ** 2 - 1)

questions.concept_tag: Number System - least number to add for divisibility
questions.question_text: What is the least number that must be added to 1,000 so that the sum is exactly divisible by 24?
questions.trap_type: Used remainder instead of divisor minus remainder
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 1,000 ÷ 24 gives quotient 41 and remainder 16. The next multiple of 24 is 24 × 42 = 1,008, so the number to add is 24 - 16 = 8. Shortcut: number to add = divisor - remainder. Trap (B): 16 is the remainder itself, which is what you would subtract, not add. Trap (C): 41 is the quotient. Trap (D): 1,008 is the resulting sum, not the number to be added.
questions.verify_code: answer = next(n for n in range(24) if (1000 + n) % 24 == 0)

questions.concept_tag: Mensuration - revolutions of a wheel
questions.question_text: The radius of a wheel is 35 cm. How many complete revolutions does it make to cover 220 m? (Take π = 22/7)
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Circumference = 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × 35 = 220 cm = 2.2 m. Revolutions = 220 m ÷ 2.2 m = 100. Shortcut: for r = 35 (a multiple of 7), the circumference is 220 cm, so 22,000 cm ÷ 220 cm = 100. Trap (A): 1 compares 220 m with 220 cm without converting units. Trap (B): 200 uses πr = 110 cm as the circumference. Trap (D): 10 converts 220 m into 2,200 cm, a slip of a factor of 10.
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
circ_cm = 2 * Fraction(22, 7) * 35
answer = Fraction(22000) / circ_cm

questions.concept_tag: Ratio - ages from the age difference
questions.question_text: The present ages of a father and his son are in the ratio 7 : 2. If the father is 35 years older than the son, what is the father's present age?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The ratio is 7 : 2, so the difference is 5 parts = 35 years and one part = 7 years. Father = 7 × 7 = 49 years (the son is 14). Shortcut: father = difference × 7/5 = 35 × 7/5. Trap (A): 14 is the son's age, not the father's. Trap (C): 35 is just the age difference. Trap (D): 63 multiplies the sum of the ratio terms (9) by the part value 7.

questions.concept_tag: Algebra - difference of squares
questions.question_text: What is the value of 17² - 13²?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 17² - 13² = (17 - 13)(17 + 13) = 4 × 30 = 120. Shortcut: use a² - b² = (a - b)(a + b) instead of squaring both numbers. Trap (A): 16 squares the difference, (17 - 13)². Trap (B): 4 stops after finding the difference. Trap (D): 30 stops after finding the sum.

questions.concept_tag: Time, Speed & Distance - speed with time in minutes
questions.question_text: A cyclist covers 30 km in 40 minutes. What is the speed of the cyclist in km/h?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 40 minutes = 2/3 hour, so speed = 30 ÷ (2/3) = 45 km/h. Shortcut: 30 km in 40 min means in 60 min the cyclist covers 30 × 60/40 = 45 km. Trap (A): 0.75 is the speed in km per minute and was never converted to km/h. Trap (B): 75 treats 40 minutes as 0.4 hour (30 ÷ 0.4). Trap (C): 30 ignores the time and reads the distance as the hourly speed.

questions.concept_tag: Boats & Streams - still-water speed from upstream
questions.question_text: A boat takes 3 hours to go 24 km upstream. If the speed of the stream is 2 km/h, what is the speed of the boat in still water?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Upstream speed = 24 ÷ 3 = 8 km/h, which equals boat speed - stream speed. So boat speed = 8 + 2 = 10 km/h. Shortcut: still-water speed = upstream speed + stream speed. Trap (B): 8 is the upstream speed itself. Trap (C): 6 subtracts the stream (8 - 2) instead of adding it. Trap (D): 12 is the downstream speed (10 + 2), not the still-water speed.
questions.verify_code: answer = 24 // 3 + 2

questions.concept_tag: Mixtures - quantity of one component from a ratio
questions.question_text: A 40-litre mixture of milk and water has the two in the ratio 3 : 2. How many litres of milk does it contain?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total parts = 3 + 2 = 5, so one part = 40 ÷ 5 = 8 litres. Milk = 3 × 8 = 24 litres. Shortcut: milk is 3/5 of the mixture, and 3/5 of 40 = 24. Trap (A): 16 is the water (2 parts), not the milk. Trap (C): 60 multiplies 40 by 3/2, treating the ratio as a scale factor on the whole mixture. Trap (D): 120 multiplies 40 by 3 without dividing by the total number of parts.

questions.concept_tag: Percentages - successive spending on changing bases
questions.question_text: A man spends 20% of his monthly income on rent and then 30% of the remaining amount on food. After these two expenses he is left with ₹5,600. What is his monthly income?
questions.trap_type: Percentage taken on the wrong base
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let the income be I. After rent, 80% of I remains. Food takes 30% of that, so 70% of 0.8I remains: 0.8I × 0.7 = 0.56I = 5,600, hence I = 10,000. Shortcut: remaining fraction = 4/5 × 7/10 = 14/25, so I = 5,600 × 25/14 = 10,000. Trap (A): 11,200 treats food as 30% of the whole income (20% + 30% = 50% spent, so 0.5I = 5,600). Trap (B): 7,000 ignores the food expense and sets 0.8I = 5,600. Trap (D): 8,736 multiplies the leftover by 1.2 and then 1.3, undoing the percentages by multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.concept_tag: Profit & Loss - buying and selling both at a discount
questions.question_text: A trader buys goods at a discount of 20% on the marked price and sells them at a discount of 10% on the same marked price. What is his profit percentage?
questions.trap_type: Profit taken on the wrong base
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Take the marked price as 100. Cost = 80 (20% discount) and selling price = 90 (10% discount), so profit = 10 on a cost of 80, i.e. 10/80 × 100 = 12.5%. Shortcut: profit % = (gap between the discounts) ÷ (100 − buying discount) × 100. Trap (B): 10% is the gap between the discounts read directly as a percentage, though the base is the cost, not the marked price. Trap (C): 11.1% divides the profit by the selling price (10/90). Trap (D): 90% is only the selling price as a percentage of the marked price.

cp = Fraction(80)
sp = Fraction(90)
answer = (sp - cp) / cp * 100

questions.trap_type: Subtracted the wrong amount of interest

Principal = amount after 2 years − interest for 2 years = 1,260 − 180 = ₹1,080. Shortcut: principal = A₂ − 2 × (yearly interest). Trap (A): 1,170 subtracts only one year's interest (90) from 1,260. Trap (B): 900 reads 180 as a single year's interest and subtracts 2 × 180 = 360. Trap (C): 1,350 takes the average of the two amounts as the principal.

questions.concept_tag: Averages - correcting wrongly entered values
questions.question_text: The average marks of 40 students were calculated as 72. Later it was found that one student's mark had been entered as 96 instead of 69, and another student's mark as 45 instead of 54. What is the correct average?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Wrong total = 40 × 72 = 2,880. The first correction lowers the total by 96 − 69 = 27, the second raises it by 54 − 45 = 9, so the net change is −18 and the correct total = 2,862. Correct average = 2,862 ÷ 40 = 71.55. Shortcut: the average moves by (net error) ÷ 40 = −18/40 = −0.45, so 72 − 0.45 = 71.55. Trap (A): 72.45 gets the direction of the net correction wrong (+0.45). Trap (C): 71.325 corrects only the first entry (−27/40 = −0.675). Trap (D): 71.1 adds the two error sizes (27 + 9 = 36) as if both lowered the total (−0.9).
questions.verify_code:
from fractions import Fraction
answer = Fraction(40 * 72 - 27 + 9, 40)

questions.concept_tag: Time & Work - whole-job days from part-job data
questions.question_text: A can do 1/3 of a piece of work in 5 days and B can do 2/5 of the same work in 10 days. In how many days can they finish the whole work together?
questions.trap_type: Part of a job treated as the whole job
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A alone: 5 ÷ (1/3) = 15 days. B alone: 10 ÷ (2/5) = 25 days. Together they do 1/15 + 1/25 = 5/75 + 3/75 = 8/75 of the work per day, so the whole work takes 75/8 = 9.375 days. Shortcut: take total work = 75 units; A does 5 units a day, B does 3, together 8 units a day. Trap (A): 3.33 treats the partial jobs as complete jobs (5 and 10 days), giving 1/(1/5 + 1/10) = 10/3. Trap (C): 20 is the average of 15 and 25; working together must beat the faster worker. Trap (D): 40 adds 15 and 25.

a = Fraction(5) / Fraction(1, 3)
b = Fraction(10) / Fraction(2, 5)

questions.concept_tag: Time, Speed & Distance - train length from platform and pole times
questions.question_text: A train takes 30 seconds to cross a platform 300 m long and 20 seconds to cross a pole standing on the platform. What is the length of the train?
questions.trap_type: Train length ignored in platform crossing
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The only difference between the two crossings is the platform: the extra 30 − 20 = 10 seconds are spent covering 300 m. So speed = 300 ÷ 10 = 30 m/s. Crossing the pole means covering the train's own length in 20 seconds, so length = 30 × 20 = 600 m. Check: train + platform = 900 m = 30 m/s × 30 s. Shortcut: speed = platform length ÷ (difference of the two times). Trap (A): 900 m is the distance covered while crossing the platform (train + platform), not the train. Trap (B): 300 m is just the platform length. Trap (D): 200 m uses speed = 300 ÷ 30 = 10 m/s, forgetting that the train must also clear its own length.

questions.concept_tag: Mensuration - recasting a sphere into cones
questions.question_text: A solid metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into small solid cones, each of base radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. How many cones are obtained?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Volume is conserved. Sphere = (4/3)π(6)³ = 288π. Cone = (1/3)π(3)²(4) = 12π. Number of cones = 288π ÷ 12π = 24. Shortcut: π cancels, so compute (4/3 × 216) ÷ (1/3 × 9 × 4) = 288 ÷ 12. Trap (A): 8 uses the cone volume without the 1/3 factor (36π), giving 288 ÷ 36. Trap (B): 18 uses the sphere volume without the 4/3 factor (216π ÷ 12π). Trap (C): 192 takes the diameter 12 cm as the radius of the sphere, giving (4/3)(12)³ = 2,304 and 2,304 ÷ 12.

cone = Fraction(1, 3) * 3 ** 2 * 4
answer = sphere / cone

questions.concept_tag: Simplification - nested fraction
questions.question_text: What is the value of 1 + 1/(1 + 1/(1 + 1/2))?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Work from the innermost bracket outwards. 1 + 1/2 = 3/2. Then 1/(3/2) = 2/3, so the next bracket is 1 + 2/3 = 5/3. Then 1/(5/3) = 3/5, so the whole expression is 1 + 3/5 = 8/5. Shortcut: at each level flip the previous result and add 1 (3/2 → 5/3 → 8/5). Trap (B): 5/8 inverts the final answer instead of adding it to 1. Trap (C): 5/3 stops after the second level and misses the outermost 1 + 1/(...). Trap (D): 3/2 stops after the innermost bracket.

inner = 1 + Fraction(1, 2)
mid = 1 + 1 / inner
answer = 1 + 1 / mid

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Take B = 100. Then A = 80 and C = 125. C exceeds A by 45, and the base is A (the salary being compared with), so the excess is 45/80 × 100 = 56.25%. Shortcut: C/A = 1.25/0.8 = 25/16, so C is 9/16 = 56.25% more than A. Trap (A): 45% reads the gap of 45 (or 20 + 25) directly as a percentage. Trap (B): 36% divides the gap by C (45/125) instead of by A. Trap (D): 5% subtracts the two percentages (25 − 20).

a = Fraction(4, 5)
c = Fraction(5, 4)
answer = (c - a) / a * 100

questions.concept_tag: Ratio - income, expenditure and equal savings
questions.question_text: The incomes of A and B are in the ratio 5 : 4 and their expenditures are in the ratio 3 : 2. If each of them saves ₹1,600, what is A's income?
questions.trap_type: Savings taken as one ratio part
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let the incomes be 5x and 4x and the expenditures 3k and 2k. Savings: 5x − 3k = 1,600 and 4x − 2k = 1,600. Multiply the second equation by 3/2 to get 6x − 3k = 2,400, then subtract the first equation: x = 800. So A's income = 5 × 800 = ₹4,000 (k = 800, so A spends 2,400, B earns 3,200 and spends 1,600). Shortcut: scale one equation so the expenditure terms match, then subtract. Trap (A): ₹3,200 is B's income. Trap (B): ₹2,400 is A's expenditure. Trap (C): ₹8,000 treats the savings as one ratio part and multiplies 5 × 1,600.

questions.question_text: ₹6,000 is lent in two parts, one at 5% and the other at 8% simple interest per annum. The total interest for one year is ₹405. What is the sum lent at 5%?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Mean rate = 405/6,000 = 6.75%. By alligation, (amount at 5%) : (amount at 8%) = (8 − 6.75) : (6.75 − 5) = 1.25 : 1.75 = 5 : 7. So the part at 5% = 5/12 × 6,000 = ₹2,500. Check: 2,500 × 5% = 125 and 3,500 × 8% = 280, total 405. Shortcut: the mean rate lies closer to the rate that carries more money, so the amount at 5% is the smaller part. Trap (A): 3,500 reverses the alligation ratio and gives the amount at 8%. Trap (C): 3,000 assumes the sum is split equally. Trap (D): 3,750 takes 5/8 of 6,000, using the wrong total (8) for the ratio 5 : 7.

questions.concept_tag: Profit & Loss - profit given as a percentage of selling price
questions.question_text: On an article, the profit is 20% of its selling price. What is the profit percentage on its cost price?
questions.trap_type: Profit taken on the wrong base

Shortcut: if profit is p% of SP, profit on cost = p/(100 − p) × 100 = 20/80 × 100. Trap (A): 20% reads the given percentage as profit on cost, but the stated base is the selling price. Trap (B): 80% is the cost price as a percentage of the selling price. Trap (D): 125% is the selling price as a percentage of the cost price, not the profit.

profit = Fraction(20)

questions.concept_tag: Time, Speed & Distance - chase with a head start
questions.question_text: A policeman sees a thief 100 m ahead of him. The thief runs at 8 m/s and the policeman chases at 10 m/s. How far does the thief run before being caught?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The policeman gains 10 − 8 = 2 m every second, so closing the 100 m gap takes 100 ÷ 2 = 50 s. In that time the thief runs 8 × 50 = 400 m. Check: the policeman runs 10 × 50 = 500 m = 400 m + 100 m head start. Shortcut: thief's distance = gap × (thief's speed) ÷ (difference of speeds) = 100 × 8 ÷ 2. Trap (B): 500 m is the distance run by the policeman. Trap (C): 800 m multiplies the gap by the thief's speed (100 × 8) and forgets to divide by the speed difference. Trap (D): 50 is the time in seconds, not a distance.

time = gap // (10 - 8)
answer = 8 * time

questions.concept_tag: Number System - largest n-digit multiple of several numbers
questions.question_text: What is the largest 4-digit number that is exactly divisible by 15, 18 and 24?
questions.trap_type: Used the LCM of only two of the numbers
questions.pedagogical_explanation: LCM: 15 = 3 × 5, 18 = 2 × 3², 24 = 2³ × 3, so LCM = 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360. The largest 4-digit number is 9,999; 9,999 ÷ 360 leaves remainder 279, so the answer is 9,999 − 279 = 9,720 (= 27 × 360). Shortcut: largest n-digit number minus its remainder on division by the LCM. Trap (A): 9,360 steps back one multiple of 360 too many (26 × 360). Trap (C): 9,990 is the answer for 15 and 18 only (LCM 90); it is not divisible by 24. Trap (D): 10,080 is the next multiple of 360, which has 5 digits.
questions.verify_code: answer = max(n for n in range(1000, 10000) if n % 15 == 0 and n % 18 == 0 and n % 24 == 0)

questions.concept_tag: Number System - remainder under a smaller divisor
questions.question_text: A number leaves a remainder of 29 when divided by 56. What is the remainder when the same number is divided by 8?
questions.trap_type: Assumed the remainder stays the same
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Write the number as N = 56k + 29. Since 8 divides 56, the part 56k is a multiple of 8, so the remainder on division by 8 is the remainder of 29 on division by 8, which is 5 (29 = 3 × 8 + 5). Shortcut: when the new divisor is a factor of the old one, reduce the old remainder by the new divisor. Trap (A): 29 assumes the remainder is unchanged, but a remainder must be smaller than the divisor 8. Trap (B): 1 divides by 7 (the other factor of 56) instead of 8. Trap (C): 0 assumes N is divisible by 8 just because 8 divides 56, ignoring the leftover 29.
questions.verify_code:
n = 56 * 5 + 29
answer = n % 8

questions.concept_tag: Mensuration - area of a path around a rectangle
questions.question_text: A rectangular park is 60 m long and 40 m wide. A path 2.5 m wide runs all around it on the outside. What is the area of the path?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The path is outside, so the outer rectangle is (60 + 2 × 2.5) by (40 + 2 × 2.5) = 65 m by 45 m, with area 2,925 m². The park is 60 × 40 = 2,400 m². Path = 2,925 − 2,400 = 525 m². Shortcut: path area = 2w(l + b + 2w) = 5 × (100 + 5) = 525. Trap (B): 500 multiplies the park's perimeter by the width (200 × 2.5) and misses the four corner squares of 2.5 × 2.5. Trap (C): 475 treats the path as running inside the park (2,400 − 55 × 35). Trap (D): 2,925 stops at the area of the outer rectangle.

questions.question_text: The population of a town increases by 10% every year. If its present population is 53,240, what was its population 3 years ago?
questions.trap_type: Applied a decrease instead of dividing by the growth factor
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Three years of 10% growth multiply the population by 1.1³ = 1.331. So P × 1.331 = 53,240 and P = 53,240 ÷ 1.331 = 40,000. Shortcut: 1.331 = 1,331/1,000 and 53,240 = 40 × 1,331, so P = 40 × 1,000. Trap (A): 37,268 takes 30% off the present figure (53,240 × 0.7). Trap (C): 38,812 reduces by 10% three times in a row (53,240 × 0.9³), but a 10% fall does not undo a 10% rise. Trap (D): 40,954 divides by 1.3, treating three years of growth as a simple 30%.

answer = Fraction(53240) / Fraction(11, 10) ** 3

questions.concept_tag: Compound Interest - half-yearly compounding
questions.question_text: What is the amount on ₹16,000 for 1 year at 20% per annum, compounded half-yearly?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Half-yearly compounding halves the rate and doubles the number of periods: rate = 10% per half-year, periods = 2. Amount = 16,000 × 1.1 × 1.1 = ₹19,360. Shortcut: two successive 10% rises equal a 21% rise, so 16,000 × 1.21. Trap (A): 19,200 compounds annually for 1 year (16,000 × 1.2). Trap (B): 17,600 applies only one half-year period (16,000 × 1.1). Trap (C): 23,040 uses the full 20% in each of the two half-years (16,000 × 1.2²).

answer = 16000 * Fraction(11, 10) ** 2

questions.concept_tag: Number System - factor needed to make a perfect cube
questions.question_text: What is the smallest number by which 1,512 must be multiplied so that the product is a perfect cube?
questions.trap_type: Whole cube instead of the missing power
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Factorise: 1,512 = 8 × 189 = 2³ × 3³ × 7. A perfect cube needs every prime exponent to be a multiple of 3. The primes 2 and 3 already have exponent 3, but 7 has exponent 1, so two more 7s are needed: multiply by 7² = 49. The product is 74,088 = 42³. Shortcut: prime-factorise, then for each prime with exponent e (not a multiple of 3) multiply by that prime to the power (3 − e mod 3). Trap (A): 7 supplies only one more factor of 7, giving 7² in the product, which is still not a cube. Trap (B): 343 = 7³ multiplies by a whole cube of 7 instead of the missing 7². Trap (D): 189 is what is left of 1,512 after removing the cube 2³; it is not the missing factor.
questions.verify_code: answer = next(m for m in range(1, 1000) if any(k ** 3 == 1512 * m for k in range(1, 200)))

questions.concept_tag: Time & Work - wages in proportion to work done
questions.question_text: A can finish a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. With the help of C they finish it in 5 days and are paid ₹3,000 in all, shared in proportion to the work each did. What is C's share?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A and B together do 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 of the job per day. All three finish in 5 days, so the combined rate is 1/5 per day and C's rate = 1/5 - 1/6 = 1/30. In 5 days C does 5/30 = 1/6 of the whole job, so C's share = 3,000 ÷ 6 = ₹500. Shortcut: the rates are in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1 (1/10 : 1/15 : 1/30 = 3/30 : 2/30 : 1/30), and since they all worked the same 5 days, the pay splits 3 : 2 : 1, so C gets 1/6. Trap (B): ₹1,000 splits the money equally among three people. Trap (C): ₹600 takes the combined rate 1/5 as C's work, so C gets 1/5 of the pay. Trap (D): ₹1,500 is A's share (A did half the job), not C's.

a = Fraction(1, 10)
b = Fraction(1, 15)
total = Fraction(1, 5)
c = total - a - b
answer = 3000 * c / total

questions.concept_tag: Boats & Streams - distance from the two journey times
questions.question_text: A boat takes 4 hours to go a certain distance downstream and 6 hours to return the same distance upstream. If the speed of the stream is 3 km/h, what is the distance?
questions.trap_type: Stream speed used once instead of twice
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Downstream speed = D/4 and upstream speed = D/6. Their difference is twice the stream speed: D/4 - D/6 = 2 × 3 = 6, so D/12 = 6 and D = 72 km. Check: downstream 18 km/h, upstream 12 km/h, boat 15 km/h, stream 3 km/h. Shortcut: downstream speed - upstream speed = 2 × stream speed. Trap (A): 36 sets D/4 - D/6 = 3, using the stream speed once instead of twice. Trap (C): 144 is the length of the round trip (72 + 72). Trap (D): 60 multiplies the still-water speed 15 km/h by the downstream time 4 h.
questions.verify_code: answer = next(D for D in range(1, 500) if 3 * D - 2 * D == 72)

questions.concept_tag: Averages - replacing a member
questions.question_text: In a committee, a member aged 58 is replaced by a new member aged 28, and the average age of the committee falls by 2 years. How many members are there in the committee?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The replacement lowers the total age by 58 - 28 = 30 years. The average falls by 2, so n × 2 = 30 and n = 15. Shortcut: number of members = (change in total) ÷ (change in average). Trap (A): 60 multiplies 30 × 2 instead of dividing. Trap (B): 16 counts the new member as an extra person (15 + 1), though he only replaced someone. Trap (D): 43 averages the two ages, (58 + 28) ÷ 2, instead of using their difference.

questions.concept_tag: Simplification - surds and reciprocals
questions.question_text: If x = √3 + √2, what is the value of x² + 1/x²?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Since (√3 + √2)(√3 - √2) = 3 - 2 = 1, we get 1/x = √3 - √2. Then x + 1/x = 2√3 and (x + 1/x)² = 12. So x² + 1/x² = 12 - 2 = 10. Direct check: x² = 5 + 2√6 and 1/x² = 5 - 2√6, which add to 10. Shortcut: x² + 1/x² = (x + 1/x)² - 2. Trap (A): 12 stops at (x + 1/x)² and forgets to subtract 2. Trap (B): 5 keeps only the rational part of x² and never adds 1/x². Trap (C): 14 adds 2 instead of subtracting it.

questions.concept_tag: Geometry - angle between two angle bisectors
questions.question_text: In triangle ABC, ∠A = 70°. The bisectors of ∠B and ∠C meet at the point O. What is the measure of ∠BOC?
questions.trap_type: Wrong sign in the bisector formula
questions.pedagogical_explanation: ∠B + ∠C = 180° - 70° = 110°. The bisectors give ∠OBC + ∠OCB = 110° ÷ 2 = 55°. In triangle BOC, ∠BOC = 180° - 55° = 125°. Shortcut: the angle between two internal bisectors is 90° + (third angle)/2 = 90° + 35° = 125°. Trap (B): 110° is ∠B + ∠C, before halving. Trap (C): 55° is ∠OBC + ∠OCB, which was never subtracted from 180°. Trap (D): 145° subtracts half of ∠A (35°) from 180° (180° - 35°) instead of using the 55° half-sum of ∠B and ∠C.

questions.concept_tag: Mensuration - cylinder volume after changing radius and height
questions.question_text: The radius of a cylinder is increased by 20% and its height is decreased by 25%. By what percent does its volume change?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Volume = πr²h. New volume factor = (1.2)² × 0.75 = 1.44 × 0.75 = 1.08, so the volume rises by 8%. Shortcut: 6/5 × 6/5 × 3/4 = 27/25 = 1.08. Trap (A): 5% decrease adds the percentages directly (+20 - 25 = -5). Trap (B): 10% decrease forgets that r is squared (1.2 × 0.75 = 0.9). Trap (D): 19% increase adds the squared effect of r as 44% and then subtracts 25% (44 - 25 = 19) instead of multiplying the factors.

questions.concept_tag: Simple Interest - time to reach a larger multiple
questions.question_text: A sum of money becomes 3 times itself in 12 years at simple interest. In how many years will it become 5 times itself at the same rate?
questions.trap_type: Amount multiple used instead of interest multiple
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Becoming 3 times means the interest is 2P (amount 3P minus principal P), earned in 12 years, so the interest per P of principal takes 6 years. Becoming 5 times needs interest 4P, which takes 4 × 6 = 24 years. Shortcut: time ∝ (multiple - 1), so 12 × (5 - 1)/(3 - 1) = 24. Trap (A): 20 scales the time with the amounts (12 × 5/3). Trap (B): 30 uses the interest multiple as 5P instead of 4P (12 × 5/2). Trap (C): 36 multiplies the time by 3 (12 × 3).

questions.concept_tag: Number System - digit sum of a number and its reverse
questions.question_text: The sum of a two-digit number and the number formed by reversing its digits is 143. If the tens digit is 3 more than the units digit, what is the number?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: For digits a (tens) and b (units): (10a + b) + (10b + a) = 11(a + b) = 143, so a + b = 13. With a - b = 3, a = 8 and b = 5, so the number is 85 (and 85 + 58 = 143). Shortcut: the sum of a number and its reverse is always 11 × (digit sum), so divide 143 by 11 first. Trap (A): 58 has the right digit sum but the tens digit is smaller, so it is the reversed number. Trap (C): 94 has digit sum 13 but the digits differ by 5, not 3. Trap (D): 76 has digit sum 13 but the digits differ by 1, not 3.
questions.verify_code: answer = next(n for n in range(10, 100) if n + (n % 10) * 10 + n // 10 == 143 and n // 10 - n % 10 == 3)

questions.concept_tag: Time, Speed & Distance - mixed modes of travel
questions.question_text: A man covers a journey of 84 km in 6 hours, partly by bus at 30 km/h and the rest on foot at 6 km/h. For how long does he walk?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Let him walk for t hours, so he rides for 6 - t hours: 30(6 - t) + 6t = 84, which gives 180 - 24t = 84 and t = 4 hours. Shortcut (assume all by bus): 6 h × 30 km/h = 180 km, which is 96 km too much; each hour of walking instead of riding cuts 24 km, so he walked 96 ÷ 24 = 4 hours. Trap (B): 2 hours is the time spent on the bus, not on foot. Trap (C): 3 hours assumes the time is split equally, but then the distance would be 108 km. Trap (D): 14 hours is the time for the whole 84 km on foot (84 ÷ 6).
